q:
**Trauma epidemiology:**
a Burden
b Classic pattern
c Current pattern
d The two leading causes of trauma death
a:
a Over **5 million** deaths a year worldwide; a leading cause of
death in the young (15–29).
b **Trimodal**: immediate (at scene), early (hours: bleeding,
brain), late (days–weeks: sepsis, organ failure).
c With modern systems, **bimodal**: early (neurological injury,
blood loss) and late (organ dysfunction).
d **Blood loss** and **neurological injury**.

- **AIS 3 or more** in **2 or more** body regions, **plus 1 or more** of:
- **Hypotension**: SBP 90 mmHg or less.
- **Coagulopathy**: INR 1.4 or more, or APTT 40 s or more.
- **GCS 8 or less**.
- **Base excess −6 or worse**.
- **Age 70 or more**.

Over 40 earlier definitions (number of injuries, ISS, mechanism, systemic
response). Older one: 2+ severe injuries of head, chest or abdomen, or one
plus an extremity injury.

q: **Primary survey: C, D, E and adjuncts.**
a:
- **C**: hypotension after injury = **bleeding until proven otherwise**;
palpable radial pulse ≈ SBP 70 (your notes), carotid ≈ 60; find
the source (**eFAST**, CT angiography); large-bore IV; blood gas
and Hb at the bedside.
- **D**: GCS (mild 13–14 in notes, standard 13–15; moderate 9–12;
severe 8 or less); pupils (one dilated = ipsilateral herniation;
both = brainstem herniation, toxins, hypotension); lateralising
signs; spinal level.
- **E**: undress fully; **prevent hypothermia**.
- **Adjuncts**: ECG, SpO₂, **capnography**, ABG, urinary and gastric
catheters, chest X-ray, eFAST, DPL.
- **Secondary survey**: AMPLE history, head-to-toe, trauma CT.
watch:
ATLS teaching is radial ≈ 80, femoral ≈ 70, carotid ≈ 60 mmHg; all
overestimate *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*. eFAST adds both
pleural windows (pneumo- and haemothorax) to FAST.

a:
1. Control **massive external bleeding** first.
2. Basic airway manoeuvres; intubate immediately only for
dangerous hypoxia or a dynamic airway injury.
3. Look for occult shock: **SBP under 110**, **shock index over 1**
(HR ÷ SBP), flat IVC with bleeding, **lactate over 4 or base**
**deficit over 6**, loss of central pulses, cold limbs.
4. Shock: **blood products and TXA**, bind the pelvis,
decompress the chest, treat tamponade; vasopressors if
neurogenic shock.
5. Then intubate with **25–50% of the usual induction dose** and
a **full paralytic dose**; watch for peri-intubation collapse.
watch:
Intubating a bleeding patient before filling the tank causes arrest: positive
pressure and induction drugs remove the remaining preload and tone.

q:
**The lethal triad:**
a The triad
b Independent predictors of death
c Hypothermia
d Acidosis
a:
- a **Hypothermia** (under 34 °C), **acidosis** (pH under 7.2), **coagulopathy**: each worsens the others; all three = very high mortality.
- b pH under 7.1 (**OR 12.3**), temperature under 34 °C (OR 8.7), ISS over 25 (OR 7.7), SBP under 70; all four ≈ 98% mortality.
- c Lost thermoregulation, no shivering, low metabolism, cold fluids, exposure; core under **32 °C** in trauma ≈ **100% mortality**.
- d Poor perfusion, **saline** resuscitation; factor VIIa, Xa/Va complex and platelets fail; myocardial depression.

- **Early (endogenous, acute traumatic coagulopathy)**: tissue injury exposes endothelium; **shock activates protein C** (anticoagulation) and **hyperfibrinolysis**; **fibrinogen falls first**.
- **Late (iatrogenic)**: consumption, **dilution** with clot-free fluids, hypothermia, acidosis.
Six drivers: tissue damage, shock, inflammation, hypothermia, acidosis, haemodilution.
watch: Also called acute traumatic coagulopathy or ACoTS. Present on arrival in about a quarter of severely injured patients, before any fluid *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*: hence early plasma, fibrinogen and TXA.

q:
**Lactate and base excess in trauma:**
a Lactate
b Pitfall
c Base excess
a:
- a **Initial lactate and 6-h clearance** independently predict death; over 3 mmol/L: sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.73 for 24-h mortality.
- b **Alcohol** raises it.
- c **Base excess** is the better biochemical predictor: mild −2 to −5, moderate −6 to −9, **severe −10 or worse**.

**ANATOMICAL** | **PHYSIOLOGICAL** | **LABORATORY**
**ISS over 36** | Weak or absent radial pulse | Lactate over 2.5 mmol/L
**Penetrating abdomen or chest** | **Core under 35 °C** | Platelets under 90,000
**Open pelvic fracture** | **SBP under 100**; HR over 100 | Fibrinogen under 1 g/L
**Long bone + head injury or lung contusion** | P/F under 250 | PT over 16 s, INR over 1.5
**Truncal haemorrhage, amputation** | Urine under 50 mL/h | Hb under 11; pH under 7.2
watch: Your notes print "fibrinogen > 1 g/dL"; it is LOW fibrinogen (under 1 g/L) that triggers damage control.

a:
- **Permissive hypotension**: SBP 70–90 (or MAP 50), normal mentation, palpable pulses, until bleeding is controlled; follow lactate and ScvO₂.
- **Not in TBI or spinal cord injury**: keep **MAP 80 or more** if GCS 8 or less.
- **Restrict crystalloid**: big volumes worsen bleeding (dilution, clot disruption), oedema, hepatocellular injury.
- **Haemostatic resuscitation**: blood products first, **RBC:FFP:platelets about 1:1:1**.
Penetrating torso: restrictive policy (SBP 60–70) lowers bleeding and 28-day mortality.
watch: Blood is the only colloid used in trauma: HES increases AKI and mortality; gelatin causes anaphylaxis; hypertonic saline only for raised ICP.

q:
**Damage control surgery, rewarming, bleeding control:**
a Damage control surgery
b Rewarming
c Haemorrhage control
d Aortic occlusion
a:
- a Temporary sacrifice of anatomy to save physiology: **(1)** **abbreviated laparotomy** (control bleeding and contamination), **(2) ICU resuscitation**, **(3) planned** **re-operation** for definitive repair.
- b Passive external (blankets, warm room); active external (**forced air**); active internal (**warm IV fluids**, warm peritoneal lavage).
- c **Pelvic binder**, compressive dressings, **tourniquets**; surgery is the gold standard; **interventional radiology**; pelvic packing or embolisation if unstable despite a binder.
- d **REBOA**: balloon in the aorta; **zone 3** (infrarenal to bifurcation; notes: IMA to bifurcation) for pelvic bleeding; **zone 1** (descending thoracic) for abdominal bleeding *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.

**TRIAL** | **COMPARISON** | **RESULT**
**SAFE** 2004 (ICU) | Saline vs 4% albumin | 28-day mortality similar
**SAFE-TBI** 2007 | Saline vs albumin in TBI | **Albumin: higher mortality** at 24 months
**FIRST 2011** (trauma) | Saline vs HES 130/0.4 | HES: less volume, lower lactate in penetrating; mortality similar
**CHEST** 2012 | Saline vs 6% HES | Mortality similar; **more RRT with** **HES**
**CRYSTAL** **2013** (shock) | Crystalloid vs colloid | 28-day mortality similar
watch: Your notes say "renal injury less with HES" for FIRST; the larger trials (CHEST, 6S) showed more kidney injury with starch *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.

q:
**Massive transfusion:**
a Definitions
b Emergency blood
c Ratio trials
d Predicting the need
a:
- a **10 or more RBC units in 24 h**; or **over 4 units in 1 h** with ongoing need; or **over 50% of blood volume in 3 h**.
- b **Group O** red cells and **group AB** plasma until the group is known.
- c **PROPPR**: 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2: no 24-h or 30-day mortality difference, but **fewer exsanguination deaths** and more haemostasis. **PROMMTT**: higher plasma and platelet ratios linked to lower early mortality.
- d **TASH** (7 variables: SBP, HR, free abdominal fluid, pelvic or long-bone fracture, sex, Hb, base excess; 0–28). **ABC score**: SBP under 90, HR over 120, penetrating, positive FAST; **2 or more → activate** *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.
watch: Exact PROPPR results are *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*. Your notes' ABC odds: 3 = 45%, 4 = 100%. Your notes list age instead of Hb in TASH; TASH 16+ → over 50% chance of massive transfusion.

a:
**STOP GIVING** | **WHEN**
**Red cells** | Hb about 10 g/dL (notes)
**FFP** | **PT under 18 s**, PTT under 35 s
**Platelets** | Count above target (notes print 150,000)
**Cryoprecipitate** | **Fibrinogen over 100 mg/dL** (1 g/L)
watch: Viscoelastic tests (TEG, ROTEM): faster, detect hyperfibrinolysis, run at body temperature, reduce transfusion; a Cochrane review found no proven mortality benefit. European targets: fibrinogen 1.5–2 g/L *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*; platelets over 50 (over 100 in TBI).

q:
**Tranexamic acid in trauma:**
a Trial and dose
b Window
c TBI
d European guidance
a:
- a **CRASH-2**: **1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h**; fewer bleeding deaths (about 15%).
- b **Within 3 h** of injury; after 3 h it increased bleeding deaths *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.
- c **CRASH-3**: benefit in **mild-to-moderate TBI** (given early), none in severe TBI.
- d Give as early as possible to anyone bleeding or at risk; prehospital first dose.
watch: Your notes say "benefit if given within the first 8 hours"; the window is 3 h (8 h is the infusion length). Your notes place the TBI result under CRASH-2; it is CRASH-3.

a:
| **FIBRINOGEN CONCENTRATE** | **CRYOPRECIPITATE**
**Source** | Lyophilised, pathogen-reduced powder | Controlled thawing of FFP
**Contains** | Fibrinogen only | **Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF**, XIII
**Dose** | (Target − measured, mg/dL) ÷ 1.7 mg/kg; often about 70 mg/kg (notes) | **1 unit per 5–10 kg**
**Pros / cons** | Fast, no matching | Availability, allogenic, thawing time, group-matched
watch: Fibrinogen falls first and furthest in bleeding trauma; concentrate lowered 6-h mortality; CRYOSTAT-1 restored levels quickly. CRYOSTAT-2 (early cryo): no mortality benefit *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*; your notes call it ongoing.

q:
**Other drugs in polytrauma:**
a Calcium
b Factor VIIa
c Steroids in spinal cord injury
d Antioxidants
a:
- a Cofactor for clotting, cardiac contractility and vascular tone; monitor every 10 units transfused; keep **ionised Ca over 0.9** **mmol/L** (notes).
- b **rFVIIa**: off-label; no outcome benefit; thrombosis; status unclear (notes); last resort only *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.
- c NASCIS II: high-dose methylprednisolone within 8 h improved motor recovery; NASCIS III: 48 h better than 24 h if started 3–8 h. **Now not recommended** (CNS, CAEP): harms, no long-term benefit.
- d Vitamins A, C, E: less inflammation; vitamin C may protect the kidneys.
watch: European guideline keeps ionised calcium in the normal range (over 1.1–1.15 mmol/L) *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.

a:
**ITEM** | **RECOMMENDATION**
**Restricted volume** **BP (no TBI)** | to target SBP 80–90 until bleeding controlled *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*
**BP (severe TBI, GCS 8 or less)** | **MAP 80 or more**
**Vasopressors** | With fluids for life-threatening hypotension
**Fluid** | **Isotonic crystalloid**; avoid excess 0.9% saline
**Haemoglobin** | **7–9 g/dL**
**Coagulation start** **Plasma:RBC at least 1:2**, or **fibrinogen concentrate** **+ RBC**
**TXA** | 1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h, **within 3 h**
**Platelets** | **Over 50**; **over 100** with ongoing bleeding or TBI

q:
**True or false?**
a BP first falls in Class II shock.
b A shock index over 1 predicts mortality.
c Permissive hypotension suits severe TBI.
d TXA helps if given up to 8 h after injury.
e Fibrinogen is the first factor to fall critically.
f Albumin is the preferred fluid in TBI.
g Berlin polytrauma needs AIS 3+ in 2+ regions plus a physiological factor.
h ISS sums the three worst injuries regardless of region.
a:
**T/F** | **REASON**
**a** | F | Class III (30–40%).
**b** | T
**c** | F | Contraindicated in TBI.
**d** | F | Within 3 h.
**e** | T
**f** | F | Higher mortality (SAFE-TBI).
**g** | T
**h** | F | One injury per region (that is NISS).
